papers.title_in_file: Subspace Controllability in Variational Quantum Circuits: Maximising Expressivity and Increasing Search Efficiency with Dynamical Lie Algebras
papers.what_it_is: A short arXiv preprint (21 Sep 2026) that tests, on a three-digit MNIST-1D classification task and over hyperparameter searches, whether subspace controllable variational quantum circuits reach lower training and validation losses than uncontrollable ones.

quotes: Our results show that over a hyperparameter search, the majority of quantum models that achieve the lowest training and validation losses are subspace controllable.
The multi-layer perceptron outperformed all models in convergence speed, generalisation accuracies and the number of successful models throughout hyperparameter searches.
For our experiments, 5,000 samples of the digits 0, 2, and 6 were generated with the accompanying Python library of MNIST-1D.
Throughout the training of all models, 10-fold cross validation was used on this set of digits.
existing.certainty_reason: Section III states the paper's own setup.

quotes: Even though our results are limited to a single classical task, they warrant further research to apply the same methods when learning other classical-based tasks.
existing.certainty_reason: Section I states the limit; Section V repeats the need for more datasets.

assertions.value: The authors define a parameterised unitary circuit as controllable on a set M when the circuit map is surjective on M, and a circuit as controllable when it is controllable on its dynamical Lie group.
quotes: is controllable on M ⊆ SU(2n) when U is surjective on M
U is said to be controllable if U is controllable on dlgU .
assertions.certainty_reason: Definitions 2 and 5 of Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors define the dynamical Lie algebra of a gate-based circuit as the span of the generators closed under exhaustive commutation.
quotes: where ⟨·⟩Lie denotes the exhaustive application of commutation operations of the elements within the set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 3 of Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors state, that for any Lie algebra and covering Lie group the dimensions of their vector spaces are equal, and use it to argue that a circuit whose generators span a smaller space cannot be controllable on the full special unitary group.
quotes: For any Lie algebra g and covering Lie group G, the dimension of their vector spaces are equal,
Therefore, V is uncontrollable on SU(2).
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard fact the paper states without proof; no proof is quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no proof of Proposition 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Pauli-string basis, with the identity removed, gives the Lie algebra su(2n) a dimension of 4n minus 1, for n qubits.
quotes: results in the vector space su(2n) having dimension 4n − 1
assertions.certainty_reason: Proposition 2 and the counting argument that follows it, Section II.A. The text layer prints the exponent flat; it is n in the exponent of 4 and of 2 in the original.

assertions.value: The authors state that a controllable circuit must have at least as many parameters as the dimension of its dynamical Lie group, which equals the dimension of its dynamical Lie algebra.
quotes: if a circuit is controllable, then the number of parameters of the circuit must at least be the dimension of dlgU , which is equal to the dimension dlaU .
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an immediate consequence of Definition 5 and Proposition 3, Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that most hardware efficient ansatz circuits in the NISQ era are uncontrollable, and that a 6 qubit circuit with 3 parameters per qubit per layer needs a minimum of 228 repeated layers to be controllable.
quotes: most HEA circuits in the NISQ era are uncontrollable.
a 6 qubit HEA circuit with 3 parameters per qubit per layer requires a minimum number of 228 repeated layers in order to be controllable.
assertions.certainty_reason: A computed count stated without its derivation in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The 228 figure is stated without a derivation in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that ansatzes with a polynomial sized dynamical Lie algebra can be simulated efficiently on classical hardware, and that an exponentially scaling algebra is conjectured to induce barren plateaus; the paper proposes to keep exponential algebras and use controllable circuits to mitigate training difficulties.
quotes: techniques exist that can efficiently simulate such polynomial DLA circuits on classical hardware [7]
it has been conjectured that an exponential DLA can induce barren plateaus [4], [23]
keep the exponentially scaling DLAs and provide the capability to mitigate difficulties in training by using controllable circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited results and a conjecture from other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for learning classical data, the data encoding must be restricted to the subset on which the circuit is controllable, or the circuit's operator space grows and the circuit may lose controllability.
quotes: the encoding must be restricted to the subset of which the circuit is controllable on.
potentially makes the circuit non-controllable.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argued design claim without a proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their modified hardware efficient ansatz has two decoupled subsystems of 4 and 2 qubits with 18 parameters per layer, and that it becomes controllable at 15 or more repeated layers.
quotes: in effect creating two subsystems with 4 and 2 qubits.
then the onset of controllability is at layer l ≥ (44 + 42 − 2)/18 = 15. Hence, our circuit ansatz is controllable when l ≥ 15.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A states the paper's own circuit and its controllability threshold.
assertions.reader_inference: The count of 18 parameters per layer appears in the paper's text and Fig. 2, not in these quotes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the logarithmic scaling encoding embeds data into SU(4) times SU(2) of the 4 and 2 qubit subsystems, and that the last 4 qubits are measured in the Z basis and mapped by a fully connected layer with bias to a 3 dimensional output followed by a softmax.
quotes: For our experiments, this balancing act resulted in an encoding that embeds data into SU(4) × SU(2).
are mapped using a fully connected layer with bias to a 3 dimensional output.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections II.C and III.A state the paper's own encoding and readout.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints SU(4) for the 4 qubit group and may differ from SU(24) elsewhere; the quote is the exact text.

assertions.value: The authors state that preprocessing averaged consecutive points into meso and macro features, reducing each sample from 40 to 20 features, of which 16 are meso and 4 are macro, and that a logistic regression showed no change in validation scores of the best trials before and after preprocessing.
quotes: This preprocessing of the image results in a dimensional reduction from 40 to 20 features, where 16 features contain the meso information, and the final 4 contain the macro.
There was no difference in the validation scores of the best trials in the hyperparameter search
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the paper's own preprocessing and its check.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum circuits were simulated without shots and without noise, with the cross entropy loss and the Adam optimiser.
quotes: The quantum circuits were simulated without shots nor noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A states the paper's own simulation scope.
assertions.reader_inference: Results hold for noiseless, shot-free simulation only.

assertions.value: The authors state that each set of circuits with a fixed number of repeated layers from 7 to 25 had a hyperparameter study of 100 randomly sampled trials, all models were trained for 100 epochs, and the top 5 models of each trial were trained for another 250 epochs on a new set of 1,000 samples with a 80/20 train and validation split.
quotes: a set of circuits were simulated where each individual set had a fixed number of repeated layers ranging from 7 to 25.
a hyperparameter study ran with 100 trails that were sampled randomly
They were all trained for 100 epochs.
the top 5 best performing models from each hyperparameter trial were selected to train for another 250 epochs on a new set of 1,000 data samples with a 80/20 train and validation split.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.B states the paper's own search design.

assertions.value: The authors report that a logistic regression on the three digits obtains a macro f1-score of 92 percent in validation, and that the multi-layer perceptron obtains scores of over 99 percent.
quotes: a logistic regression model obtains a macro f1-score in validation of 92%.
obtaining scores of over 99%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the uncontrollable hardware efficient ansatz achieved similar losses and generalisation accuracies to the controllable ansatz throughout the hyperparameter searches, and they attribute this to the encoding, which they say lies in a smaller operator space.
quotes: Although the HEA is uncontrollable throughout all tests, it consistently achieved similar losses and generalisation accuracies throughout the hyperparameter searches.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The attribution to the encoding is the authors' explanation, not a tested result.

assertions.value: The authors report that the highest test accuracies of the quantum models with the controllable ansatz ranged between 95 and 96 percent, and that the highest achieving models were consistently in their controllable regime.
quotes: the highest test accuracies for quantum models ranged between 95% and 96%.
The highest achieving models were consistently found to be in their controllable regime
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that controllable circuits reached both the lowest and the highest training losses, that learning rate 0.1 caused controllable circuits to become detrimental in finding minimum losses, and that these cases are a minority.
assertions.anchor: Section I and Section IV.B, Fig. 3
quotes: Although controllable circuits achieved the lowest losses, they also achieved the highest losses throughout their hyperparameter trials.
Despite the hyperparameter α = 0.1 causing controllable circuits to become detrimental in finding minimum losses, these are in a minority.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from figures.
assertions.reader_inference: This narrows the headline result: a minority of hyperparameter settings did worse when controllable.

assertions.value: The authors report that the validation loss increased while the training loss kept falling as parameters were added beyond the onset of controllability, with the centre of the overfitting bar at the 15th repeated layer.
quotes: the training loss continues to be minimised whilst the validation loss increases when trainable parameters are added.
This onset of overfitting, or the centre of this light bar, is at the 15th repeated layer which is at the onset of controllability.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from figures.

assertions.value: The authors report that the total sum of validation losses is minimised at the onset of controllability, and suggest this might be a computational phase transition.
quotes: the area plot shows that the total sum of losses is minimised at the onset of controllability, which might be a computational phase transition
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the phase transition is a conjecture.

assertions.value: The authors report that final validation losses of controllable circuits correlate strongly with those of circuits with more repeated layers, with a Pearson score greater than 0.96 at the point of controllability and much weaker correlations for circuits with 10 repeating layers or less.
quotes: much weaker linear correlations are found for circuits with 10 repeating layers or less
At the point of the circuits becoming controllable, the Pearsons score is greater than 0.96
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors propose a cheaper hyperparameter search that is fixed at the onset of controllability, restricted to the most performant circuits with 15 layers, and extended with additional layers, and they state that further experiments are needed to verify this.
quotes: First, one performs the hyperparameter search fixed at the onset of controllability, 15 layers in our experiments
Further experiments would need to be conducted to verify this conjecture.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.C states that the technique is an unverified conjecture.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's claim that the search can be restricted is stronger than this statement.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that for a subset of MNIST-1D the majority of models leveraged their controllability to increase the success rate in minimising both their validation and training loss over a hyperparameter sweep.
quotes: This work empirically demonstrated for a subset of MNIST1D, that the majority of models leveraged their controllability to increase the success rate in minimising both their validation and training loss over a hyperparameter sweep.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that more classical datasets are needed, and they claim, without evidence in the paper, that the results should continue to hold in more complicated cases.
quotes: the number of classical datasets for the learning task needs to be increased.
the results of this paper should continue to hold in more complicated cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim with no evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Only one task and one preprocessing were tested, so the claim is not supported by the paper's own data.
